name: Bruce protocol METs
seoDesc: Bruce protocol METs: work out V 02 max from the age and the time. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: V 02 max is what the Bruce protocol METs calculator works out, and it gets there from the age and the time. That makes it useful for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Bruce protocol METs calculator work?
sections.html:
The Bruce protocol METs calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports V 02 max in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex); then you type in the age and the time.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as male and female. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in years. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in minutes / seconds. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Bruce protocol METs calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

V 02 max=(-3 ÷ 250 × sex × (time ^ 3) + (451 ÷ 1000) × sex × (time ^ 2) − 5759 ÷ 1000 × sex × time + (187 ÷ 10) × sex + (219 ÷ 50) × time − 39 ÷ 10)
MET max=((2 ÷ 7) × (-3 ÷ 250 × sex × (time ^ 3) + (451 ÷ 1000) × sex × (time ^ 2) − 5759 ÷ 1000 × sex × time + (187 ÷ 10) × sex + (219 ÷ 50) × time − 39 ÷ 10))
Heart rate maximum=(192 − 7 ÷ 1000 × (age ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Sex set to Male and Age = 10 yrs. Working through the relationship above gives Heart rate maximum = 192.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Heart rate maximum = 192 should be roughly the size you expected from Sex set to Male and Age = 10 yrs.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Time, opening in years
  • Time, opening in minutes / seconds

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Bruce protocol METs calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the age and the time — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Bruce protocol METs calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns V 02 max, derived from the age and the time. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Bruce protocol METs calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age and the time, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter age in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Age opens in years and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Heart rate maximum = 192. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Bruce protocol METs calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
